scenes.title: Three Moments to Observe in an Attack
lines: Let us bring the same question into a fighting game.
Ky swings his sword in Guilty Gear, the opponent reacts, and Ky returns to a stance.
The bright effects attract your attention, but watch three moments separately.
The start of the action, contact with the opponent, and the transition to another action.
The sword's swing and the full duration of the attack may have different boundaries.
Street Fighter's Ken also brings his body back after a kick.
When someone asks for a faster attack, ask which interval felt slow.
Shorter preparation changes the opponent's reading time; shorter recovery changes the wait before another choice.
We observed normal-speed movement. Exact numbers require a defined basis, as in our original test.

scenes.title: Use a Shared Time Basis
lines: Before assigning numbers, practice observing different actions with the same basis.
Ky creates a projectile in the air, descends, and returns to his stance.
His pose keeps changing while the glowing projectile remains on screen.
Using the projectile's disappearance as the attack's end may give a different answer from the character's recovery.
In the next action, watch him slide along the ground and then stand up.
Projectile travel, character recovery, and one displayed video frame are different things to observe.
Write the observed beginning and end beside the number.
A shared update basis lets us compare how long we wait for different attacks.
This is why we converted twelve frames into seconds in the earlier explanation.

scenes.title: Separate Preparation and Recovery
lines: Now watch attacks that rise into the air or move toward the opponent.
Ky raises his leg, moves forward, attacks, and returns to a standing posture.
Movement alone does not prove that an attack hitbox is active at that moment.
An attacker may also keep moving after the opponent has been hit.
For an upward leap, observe the ascent separately from the landing.
A player who needs another action may be waiting for that ending.
In Ken's sequence of kicks, observe the connection between actions.
Long preparation, long recovery, and a transition into another action are separate questions.
The earlier diagram compared a separate change to preparation time.

scenes.title: Separate Visual Expression from Action Rules
lines: Guilty Gear's Sol presents strong poses and then moves into another pose.
Clear silhouettes and abrupt changes in shape contribute to the impression of movement.
Counting pose changes alone does not tell us when an attack was active.
Watch how Ky's character, weapon, and projectile effects change differently.
Light and projectiles may move while the character holds a pose.
Assuming every visible change belongs to one collision clock makes measurement confusing.
When refining expression, decide which pose should remain readable for longer.
Changing the action's preparation time requires a separate comparison.
That is why our test kept collision onset fixed while changing pose counts.

scenes.title: Observe Contact and What Follows
lines: Focus on contact with the opponent and the movement immediately afterward.
Ky's sequence shows effects at contact before connecting to another attack.
Sol's strong hit also has different impressions before contact, at impact, and when movement resumes.
That brief feeling of impact is a different question from the attack's preparation.
Distinguish large effects from moments when the character stops moving.
A moving background or effect does not prove that every combat-related clock keeps advancing.
Game state and records are needed to establish exactly what was paused.
Our test paused only the combat clock and left background time visible.
We turn a question from real gameplay into a small experiment with a defined subject.

scenes.title: Turn Observation into a Design Note
lines: Finally, turn the observed attack into a design note.
For a projectile attack, separate hand movement, projectile creation, and the return to a stance.
Record impact as another event because distance also affects it.
For a rushing attack, separate the start of movement, contact, and readiness for another action.
Then choose one interval to change in our own game.
If you change preparation, keep recovery and travel distance fixed and test the same situation again.
Video checks visible results; logs check the timing of internal rules.
If the records differ, check whether frames were miscounted or different clocks were observed.
Keep the feeling, find where it arises, and connect it to a change we can explain.
